source.author: cic
source.text: Quoniam, quae Graeci vocant, nobis perturbationes appellari magis placet quam morbos, in his explicandis veterem illam equidem Pythagorae primum, dein Platonis discriptionem sequar, qui animum in duas partes dividunt: alteram rationis participem faciunt, alteram expertem; in participe rationis ponunt tranquillitatem, id est placidam quietamque constantiam, in illa altera motus turbidos cum irae tum cupiditatis, contrarios inimicosque rationi.
source.text_original: Quoniam, quae Graeci πάθη vocant, nobis perturbationes appellari magis placet quam morbos, in his explicandis veterem illam equidem Pythagorae primum, dein Platonis discriptionem sequar, qui animum in duas partes dividunt: alteram rationis participem faciunt, alteram expertem; in participe rationis ponunt tranquillitatem, id est placidam quietamque constantiam, in illa altera motus turbidos cum irae tum cupiditatis, contrarios inimicosque rationi.
source.text_english: Since, in the case of those things which the Greeks call, it seems better to us to call perturbations rather than diseases, in explaining these I shall follow that ancient classification, first of Pythagoras, then of Plato, who divide the soul into two parts: one they make sharer in reason, the other without reason; in the part that shares in reason they place tranquility, that is, a calm and quiet steadfastness, in the other they place agitated movements, those of anger as well as of desire, opposed to reason and hostile to it.

reuse.author: hier
reuse.text: illi enim, quae Graeci appellant , nos perturbationes possumus dicere, aegritudinem uidelicet et gaudium, spem et metum, quorum duo praesentia, duo futura sunt, asserunt extirpari posse de mentibus et nullam fibram radicemque uitiorum in homine omnino residere meditatione et assidua exercitatione uirtutum.
reuse.text_original: illi enim, quae Graeci appellant πάθη, nos perturbationes possumus dicere, aegritudinem uidelicet et gaudium, spem et metum, quorum duo praesentia, duo futura sunt, asserunt extirpari posse de mentibus et nullam fibram radicemque uitiorum in homine omnino residere meditatione et assidua exercitatione uirtutum.
reuse.text_english: For they assert that those things which the Greeks call, and which we can call perturbations, namely distress and joy, hope and fear, of which two belong to the present and two to the future, can be rooted out from the mind, and that no fiber or root of vices at all remains in a man, by meditation and constant practice of the virtues.
